speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our debate takes place at a time when peace initiatives in the Middle East are occurring at a furious pace. The moves by President Sadat and Premier Begin have been called daredevil diplomacy. Now we learn that these daredevils are going to hold their second face to face meeting on Christmas Day. Can there be any greater Christmas present to the whole world than the continued movement forward to peace by these two courageous leaders? If it takes daredevil diplomacy to bring peace to an area that has so long been the reflection of the tragic vision of mankind, let us have more daredevil diplomacy.
To the Arab and Israeli diplomats who are listening to this debate I say it is not my intention to tell you how to solve the vexatious problems of the Middle East; I only want to tell you

they must be solved for the good of the world. Take back to your governments the wish, the insistence, the demand of the Canadian people that this fresh momentum for peace not be lost. The courage of Sadat and Begin has inspired the world. Our hopes have been raised that there is a way to extend justice to Jew and Arab alike. Do not allow the promise of this moment to be lost.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we must speak of Canada's responsibility in foreign policy. This debate will be useless if we offer only rhetoric to one another, if we advance impossible proposals, if we use it as a smokescreen to cover the deep divisions at home. Somehow, through this debate, we must strike a note of realism concerning Canada's place in a world that is undergoing great change. We must balance the strength and potential of Canada with the fact that we are divided in so many ways internally. We must balance our good reputation and image abroad with the fact that we are not a major power.
Yet considering all the realities of Canadian existence, there is no doubt in my mind that Canada can do much more than it is now doing to extend peace, stability and justice in the world. In fact this very exertion outwards into a world that is fractured would be of considerable help in revitalizing the Canadian spirit. The government's down-playing of foreign affairs-there was not a word on this subject in the throne speech-appears to be a confession that it cannot advance in the external arena until the internal picture is improved.
I am convinced that reaffirming a constructive role for Canada in the world community can be of considerable help in finding a renewed sense of purpose and direction for Canada. In fact the continued development of our own country demands that we pay greater attention to the role Canada should play in a changing world. This is not a simplistic notion, rather it is a reflection of the profoundness of human nature.
Human beings need goals to find happiness; and nations need goals to discover their unity. Outside the Parliament Buildings, there is a monument that says it well: "If I lose myself, I save myself." What this means, in modern terms, is that a renewed effort on our part to make Canada an international source of human rights and economic growth would be a means to create new bonds among Canadians. The internal strengthening of Canada through greater involvement in the newly-discovered realities of an interdependent world is a challenge of historic proportions to this country.
Can we respond to this challenge? Mr. Speaker, we have no choice but to respond. We do not live alone on this planet. Look at the picture of the earth sent back from space by the astronauts. That picture reveals graphically how the interests of one part of the globe are connected with the interests of all. If foreign policy has always been the pursuit of national aims and interests in the international environment, foreign policy must now strive to secure those interests by promoting the well-being of peoples and nations throughout the world. What is needed, therefore, is a reconstituted foreign policy for the
December 19, 1977

1980s that can reconcile the traditional needs of independence with the new demands of interdependence.
A policy of enlightened internationalism is a necessity. And that takes political leadership. The government has shown a disinterest in providing leadership to the Canadian people. It is time for members of this House to assert our determination to participate in the construction of a new foreign policy for the next decade. We are the ones who go across this country measuring public opinion and also helping to shape it. In 1977 I spoke in 27 Canadian communities on Canada's international role and I have found that in every community there is a creative minority of concerned Canadians who want a stronger foreign policy and more leadership from the government in this area.
The Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence ought to be an ideal instrument in the forming and dissemination of policy. But it is not utilized because of the silly rule that committees can only study what the government allows them to study. Thus this whole fall session has been wasted because the government would not provide a reference to the committee to study aid, or disarmament, or peacekeeping or indeed any of the many items that are opened up in the minister's annual report. All members know that consideration of estimates is not a time for exploring new possibilities. The subcommittee on international development which produced reports on a common fund for commodities and debt management during the past two sessions performed valuable work. Why should that work be suspended? If the government is serious about the motion before us asking us to take note of "future prospects of Canada's relationships with the other nations of the world," then at the very least it would refer the minister's annual report to the committee and let us get down to the serious work of contributing to a foreign policy for the 1980's.
Mr. Speaker, a reconstituted foreign policy should not make the mistake of the past decade-going off in all directions at once, especially when some directions contradict others. It should rest on firm foundations, rather than on a set of stop-and-go experiments. That has been the major flaw in Canada's foreign policy in the 1970s. In this decade the government, discovering interdependence, thought the best response was to plunge into new arenas to the diminishment of traditional relationships; to spend aid money in a plethora of developing countries without stopping to measure whether the aid was effective; to make great speeches at conferences outside Canada without ever explaining to the Canadian people why an enlarged foreign policy is necessary and what the government's plan is. As for Canada's votes in the United Nations, they have been such a strange mixture of yes, no and abstentions, with the emphasis on the abstentions, that they defy analysis.
Also, how are we to analyze the so-called third option policy? What positive gain has it produced? The necessary counterweights to our dependence on the U.S.-the Pacific Rim, the EEC, Latin America-have not materialized. The contractual link has yet to amount to anything beyond mere
External Affairs
statements of good will. Moreover, the search for a closer relationship with Europe was undermined thanks to the decision to reduce unilaterally our participation in NATO. The fact that this reduction was made before the conclusion of the foreign policy review made nonsense of the claim that foreign policy would determine defence policy.
Beside the fact that the government's foreign policy has been a failure in that it has accomplished none of the things it set out to do, it is no longer clear how or where our foreign policy is made. The most important agreement of the decade in Canada-U.S. relations, the Alcan Pipeline agreement, was negotiated not by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but by the government House leader. Our relations with francophone countries, which until recently have been handled adequately by External Affairs, are now being entrusted to another cabinet minister, the Minister for Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). The reasons for this have never been satisfactorily explained.
In a reconstituted foreign policy for the next decade, I favor a clear statement at the outset reaffirming a spirit of co-operation in Canada-U.S. relations, for the simple reason that our security and trade are inextricably bound up with the United States. And in the past decade a traditionally positive relationship has been strained, often needlessly. Canadians have been left to wonder if somehow Canada was getting delusions of grandeur that we could survive on this continent without the closest attachment to the U.S. A reaffirmation of Canada-U.S. relations at this moment would act as a stabilizing rudder as we steer into new waters.
Second, our traditional ties with the Commonwealth and NATO need to be reinforced. These great and time-tested associations provide a framework for Canada's interests abroad. Yet the government has given the appearance that we could treat old friends in a cavalier manner.
Only when Canadians are reassured that our attachments to the U.S., Europe and the Commonwealth will remain the anchors of a reconstituted policy, will such a new policy be understood and accepted. There must be movement forward into the complex fields of human rights, detente, the development and security of Africa, international development and disarmament. But these steps must be on firm foundations. We should be careful that we do not draw the analogy of Canada's being a bridge too far. For a bridge requires strong footings. Today those footings are not strong because the government has almost totally neglected to explain to the Canadian people whatever it is it is trying to do. No wonder Canadians are bewildered and think that Canada is wandering in a jungle at midnight without a compass.
If any final proof is needed about the confusion of purpose in Canada's foreign policy, Mr. Speaker, let us consider the sorry spectacle of CIDA officials now justifying Canada's aid budget on grounds that it is good for the Canadian economy. Is the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce so bereft of ideas to promote the sale of Canadian goods abroad that the

December 19, 1977
External Affairs
government must insist that CIDA become a sales agency? The mismanagement of the economy must be even worse than we imagined if CIDA, an agency that was started to express the humanitarian concern of Canadians for the poor of the world, is now to be used to prop up industry, trade and commerce.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, more than half of Canada's aid budget is spent on Canadian goods and services; this is called tied aid. There is nothing inherently wrong with tied aid, provided that it promotes development. However, given such factors as the high technological content of much tied aid, there is increasing evidence, which I have seen with my own eyes, that it can promote underdevelopment instead. The myth has grown up that tied aid is important to the Canadian economy. How can this possibly be true when tied aid represents only .23 per cent of our gross national product? If the government has evidence to the contrary, let it publish the evidence and stop operating CIDA in such secrecy that a "confidential" label is even put on its country reports.
To have the government now justifying CIDA on business grounds will, in fact, prevent CIDA from implementing the government's own strategy on international development that calls for increased emphasis on rural development of the poorest people.
There is a paradox in this which I will explain in this way. There is little direct commercial return to Canada in the development of health, education and marketing services in the villages where the greatest number of the poor live, and little benefit directly to people in developing countries through our emphasis on bilateral tied aid.
True aid is an investment in the long range development of people. If CIDA persists in explaining itself on grounds of immediate commercial return to Canada-when that return is insignificant anyway-it will seriously jeopardize that substantial body of public opinion that supports CIDA on the grounds that it is actually helping the poorest people.
Note well what I am about to say, Mr. Speaker. It is not the quantity of money that Canada spends through CIDA that is important in helping people, it is the quality. I would accept a cut in CIDA's over-all budget if I could spend the remainder on community development, especially the kind promoted by non-governmental organizations. Such a policy would, on the basis of my experience travelling in the Third World, help more of the poorest people in the poorest countries achieve self-reliance.
My leader today called for an independent review of the whole CIDA operation. I support that review because a fresh, objective examination of CIDA must now be made if the government is to retain the support of Canadians who want CIDA to help make self-reliant, dignified human beings out of the world's poverty stricken millions.
There are benefits to Canada through international development, properly carried out, and we should not hesitate to point them out. Vast new markets will open up through helping to develop a level of self-reliance in the people. Their purchasing
[Mr. Roche.1
power is now so low that they are not considered major markets despite their population size. Their incomes would increase, as the Secretary General of the Commonwealth, Shridath Ramphal, has noted, "from the dismantling of trade barriers and other obstacles and from a sustained expansion of their export income from primary commodities." These increased incomes would inevitably be spent on imports from the industrialized countries.
Developing a level of self-reliance in the one billion poorest people in the world is a long-range investment, and that is the essence of a policy that now ought to be advanced. On the question of measuring aid effectiveness we should thank the new North-South Institute that has analysed the deficiencies in Canada's present role. I quote their conclusion:
In summary, while Canadians in general, and Canadian policy-makers in particular, like to view Canada as being in (or close to) the vanguard of the industrial countries, this self-image is more flattering than accurate. Canada, on occasion, has taken positions that have put this country among the leaders of the north. However, as far as proceeding with in depth and innovative analyses or offering proposals that could facilitate substantive agreement between the north and south, Canada has neither called upon enough of its resources nor come close to realizing its potential.
In outlining an improved Canadian policy on international development in the 1980s, I would establish these priorities. First of all, more emphasis on fostering self-reliance in the Third World through the satisfaction of basic human needs- sufficient food, shelter, health facilities and education and a job opportunity for all. Those are the basics we are talking about, Mr. Speaker. Second, increased attention to water management and soil conservation. Third, intensified and continuous and two-way technical co-operation with developing countries. Fourth, emphasis on stabilizing the prices of commodities and manufactured goods; and improving access for Third World countries to industrialized countries' markets. Fifth, intensified efforts to help developing countries become more self-sufficient in food production and increased participation in world food programs. Sixth, domestic industrial strategies to enable Canada to produce more high technology goods needed on world markets.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in a reconstituted foreign policy can there be any subjects more necessary to highlight than stronger Canadian efforts to improve the conditions for human rights and arms control? We are holding this debate almost on the eve of Christmas. We want to celebrate the birth of Christ who came to us in the name of peace. But peace is not merely an ideal. Peace is a practical and immediate necessity arising out of the present situation where men have acquired such immense power that they are now in a position to conquer the stars or to annihilate themselves completely along with the globe on which they live. Peace is not just the absence of war; it is that set of equitable human and national relationships that promote the conditions for human dignity sought by every individual. What we are facing today is a world that is endangered by gross violations of human rights and widespread terrorism, a widening gap between the developed and developing nations, and an arms race that is out of control. That is neither a safe nor an equitable world in which to live.
December 19, 1977

No, we cannot do everything. But we can raise our voice and increase our work in the world community to root out the causes of disorder and injustices. I believe the Canadian people want their leaders to move in this direction. And we have the duty to provide such leadership through a new, coherent, comprehensive, and convincing foreign policy.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a general debate on Canada's foreign policy, but what I am going to discuss, the Arab boycott and the federal government's response to it, are as much matters of Canada's domestic policy as they are of its foreign policy.
The boycott touches on our foreign policy because it is a form of warfare by Arab states against Israel. It is as much a part of their effort to destroy Israel as their military warfare since 1948. However, Canada is not at war with Israel or with the Arab states.
Canada's official policy has been to support the existence of Israel as a free and independent state within secure and recognized borders. Therefore, when Arab countries say if Canadian firms want to trade with us they cannot trade with Israel or with other firms which trade with Israel or which are owned by or employ people who are sympathetic to it, they are trying to get Canadian companies to do something which clashes directly with Canada's official policy as a government, as a country.
When Arab countries say to Canadian firms. "If you want to trade with us you cannot have Jewish employees or owners or directors and you cannot trade with Canadian firms with shareholders or employers who are Jewish or who are sympathetic to Israel," then this conflicts directly with our federal government policy on human rights and the approach to human rights of most Canadians. It clashes with our domestic policy. It is understandable, therefore, why the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House in May, 1975:
This type of practice is alien to everything the government stands for and indeed to what in general Canadian ethics stand for.
These sentiments were not translated into any kind of concrete policy on the Arab and similar international boycotts until almost a year and a half later on October 21, 1976, when the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) presented to the House a statement of policy on such boycotts. This statement said the government opposes boycotts which attempt to have Canadians in their commercial dealings discriminate against other Canadians on the basis of origin or belief, or which attempt to have them refuse to buy or sell to countries like Israel with which Canada maintains friendly relations. However, in the statement the only measures the government said it would take to implement this policy were withholding its supporting services from dealings where Arab boycott compliance was involved and having all firms report to it for later publication any compliance by them with the boycott whether or not they sought government assistance.
External Affairs
This policy was not translated into any kind of action until the Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce issued guidelines for its implementation three months later on January 21, 1977. These guidelines, however, drew back from the commitment of the policy statement. They said reports would be drawn up only with regard to firms that approached the department for assistance.
No explanation has ever been offered to this House or to the public as to why the guidelines issued by the Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did not go as far as the government's formal policy statement which said all firms, whether they sought government assistance or not, would have to report to the government all requests they received to comply with international boycotts of a kind contrary to the government's policy statement. The guidelines also said a public report of information gathered under them will be made "semi-annually".
This meant the first report should have been made last July. This did not happen, and until questions were asked about it in the House last week there was no indication by the government when such a report would be issued to the public, if ever, and what had been holding it up until that point.
Although the wording of the policy statement and the guidelines at close reading are somewhat ambiguous on this, the press and the public generally interpreted them to mean that the reports, when made, would at the very least name those firms, about which the government was aware, that had agreed to comply with the boycott. In fact this understanding was encouraged by spokesmen for the government. For example, on February 17 of this year, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), then the parliamentary secretary to the President of Privy Council, speaking in an adjournment debate in reply to a speech made by myself, had this to say:
The reporting requirement under which the department would publicize the names of companies or individuals from whom services and support have been withdrawn or withheld for contravening the government's policy on boycotts is a responsible and practical way of reinforcing the government's policy in this area.
I want the House to note the words of the then parliamentary secretary which state clearly that the reporting requirement meant the department would be publicizing the names of companies or individuals from whom services and support had been withdrawn or withheld for contravening the government's guidelines on international boycotts.
As we know, answers given by parliamentary secretaries in adjournment debates are prepared for them by the relevant government departments as the official position of the government, and are presented by the parliamentary secretaries as such. It is understandable, therefore, that there was consternation, if not surprise, to say the least, when the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), as reported by the Globe and Mail in its December 17 issue, after telling the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) during the question period on the preceding day that the list of companies in question was "still being considered" said later, to reporters outside the House, on the same day, and I quote from the press report:

December 19, 1977
External Affairs
-he had no plans to make the list public and would not even indicate how many companies the department had found signing contracts with boycott clauses.
'You'd be open for all kinds of libel,' Mr. Horner said, because the publicity might hurt the companies' sales.
'That kind of thing when we're trying to promote world trade is something we don't want to get into.'
Here appears to be an even further narrowing-down of the seemingly meaningful policy announced by his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, on October 21, 1976. One could wonder how naming the companies the government found to be complying with the boycott could ever involve "all kinds of libel". How can it be libel when the government is simply telling the truth, that certain companies are engaging in conduct that the Prime Minister of Canada said is contrary to everything the government stands for, everything Canadian ethics stand for, and what the present Secretary of State for External Affairs later called repugnant and unacceptable?
Most Canadians want, as I do, to see Canadian trade with Arab countries and all countries greatly expanded. However, I do not think they want to see this done, nor do I, on terms which are contrary to basic Canadian ethics and concepts of human rights.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext:
It should be troubling indeed to note the inference of the reported remarks, assuming they are accurately reported, of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, that discrimination against some Canadians on the grounds of their origin, religion, beliefs, associations or that efforts that harm a friendly country are prices he is willing to pay to expand Canada's trade. If that inference is correct, and I hope it is not, it clashes with the policy of the government of which he is now a member and, more important, with the views of Canadians generally.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs took a somewhat different approach in the House the next day, last Friday. He said in effect that the list in question had not been released because the government had not yet decided how to release information it had received, particularly whether it should release the names of companies which had received requests to comply with the boycott but which had rejected those requests. He implied that there were other unresolved questions of the same order as well. This was when he was speaking to reporters later outside the House. He said that the government had not decided, according to press reports, whether to release the names of companies that had simply agreed not to ship goods on a vessel which stopped in Israel, but did not include a boycott clause in their sales contract.
One could have somewhat more sympathy for the government's position on this, if the policy statement had not yet been issued, or if it had been issued and the government was simply waiting for the guidelines to put it into effect. Almost a year and a half went by from the time the Prime Minister said that the boycott was contrary to everything the government stood for to the time the policy statement was issued. Was

there not enough time during this period to make the necessary decisions? During this period we asked when the policy would appear, we were told that cabinet was continuing to study the matter.
Are we to take it, then, that the cabinet spent a year and a half studying this matter and allowed a statement of policy on boycotts to be made, promising a mechanism for public reports, without first deciding on answers to these basic questions as to what information was to be put in these reports? Are we to take it, if this was not done by the time the policy statement was finally made on October 21, 1976, that there was not time for answers to these questions to be developed within the three months between the making of the policy statement and the later issuing of the guidelines in January 1977?
Are we to take it that there was not time to get answers to these questions in close to a year since the guidelines had been issued, even allowing almost an extra six months from the time the first report was due? Certainly, even with the many other matters that validly required the government's attention, I think there was time to reach a decision as to what information should be made public concerning what the government had learned with regard to boycott compliance by Canadian firms. I think the Canadian public should urge the government to get on with this matter and make decisions. Then if the public is not satisfied with those decisions, the government should be able to explain and justify them. Answers to those questions regarding the releasing of information troubling the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the cabinet, could be worked out in a few hours if it were decided that it had to be done.
I will offer some suggestions on how to proceed, in my usual effort to be helpful and constructive. If the government has learned of firms that simply received boycott requests, but did not agree with them, why should not their names simply be held back and tables would be published showing the number of firms receiving such requests, the nature of the requests, and the industrial sector in which the firms, receiving these requests are found. When it comes to companies that agree to ship goods on vessels not stopping at Israeli ports, the previous minister of industry, trade and commerce, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), seemed to state the government's position on this in a speech in Ottawa last April. At that time he said:
It would contravene our policy to undertake that the goods will not be carried on a blacklisted vessel or insured by a blacklisted insurance company, because that could limit the Canadian seller's freedom with other Canadian companies.
An argument could be made as a result of what the Minister of Finance said at the time when he was the minister of industry, trade and commerce that the names of such firms, along with the information on exactly what was agreed to, should be disclosed. But if a firm had agreed to nothing more, an argument could be made and possibly accepted, it could be put forward as a working hypothesis, that here too only statistical tables be published.
December 19, 1977

However is there any valid argument that the government should not publish the names of firms which agreed to boycott clauses in the sales agreements they entered into or that the names of firms that agreed to boycott clauses in the letters of credit under which they were to receive payment, should not be published? I am referring to boycott clauses, not to trade with Israel, with firms trading with Isreal, or in which firms agreed to discriminate against other Canadians. Surely not, if the words of the Prime Minister in May, 1975, and the words of the government's own policy statement a year and a half later, can be taken at face value. If the government needed more detailed guidance, surely it could take a look at the regulations on reporting which were made under the new comprehensive United States legislation forbidding all United States companies, whether they sought aid from their government or not, from complying with international boycotts like the Arab boycott.
In spite of earlier predictions, there is no evidence that this new American law is hurting United States trade with the Arab countries, or that it is embarrassing any American companies. Therefore I think the government is now in a position to make the necessary decisions on what to put into reports to be issued under its guidelines without further delay. The government should issue these reports as it has promised.
But let us bear in mind that these reports will tell very little about the impact of the boycott on Canada and Canadians. Even if the government publishes the names of every company coming to its attention that accepted the provisions of the boycott rules in any way, the Canadian people will not be given anything close to a true picture of the boycott implications for Canada. It is clear the government has not carried out its promise contained in the October 21 policy statement. I am referring to the promise to have all firms, whether or not they require government assistance, report their compliance with the boycott. Any report issued under the government's guidelines of January, 1977, cannot give a complete picture of the boycott's implications.
Among the essential tasks of our national government are the protection of our country's sovereignty and the providing of the equal protection of our laws to all residing within our borders. Unless the federal government brings forward all the necessary measures to make fully operative its October 21 policy on the Arab boycott and other international boycotts, it will not be carrying out these responsibilities in the way expected by Canadians generally. What do the guidelines issued by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce actually say? Those guidelines indicated that the government would withhold services only after transactions involving boycott compliance were actually entered into and signed. Also it would expect the reporting of boycott compliance by companies only where they approached it for assistance. These measures, in my view and in the views of many other Canadians of every origin, are largely without the kind of impact that is required.
Much government assistance comes in the form of trade promotion activities, circulation of information, the making of
External Affairs
contacts and so on, that take place before a transaction is entered into. Companies not requiring assistance from the government could continue as before in their dealings. Many, if not most, would not require such assistance. If they were subsidiaries of foreign firms, they could rely on the banking connections and the resources of their parent companies. If they are larger Canadian companies, they can rely on their own resources and banking connections. They would not be required to make any report of boycott compliance to the government. In fact such firms would not be likely to approach the government for help in the first place.
Ministers of external affairs continue to state their abhorrence and that of the government for the boycott. They continue to confirm that their views, and the views of the government, are that Israel has a right to exist within secure and defined borders.
Words are important. Generally Canadians have welcomed certain of Canada's recent votes at the United Nations, although they continue to be concerned about other votes in the form of abstentions in the United Nations and in certain of its specialized agencies. In situations like this, I would argue that action to implement words of support counts as much, if not more, than the words themselves.
All Canadians welcome the initiative to bring peace to the Middle East of President Sadat of Egypt and Prime Minister Begin of Israel, and all Canadians, I am sure, pray for the success of these initiatives. But a number of Arab states are refusing to take part in these efforts to bring peace to the Middle East. Perhaps part of the reason is that they still hope to bring about the destruction of Israel, if not through military warfare then through economic warfare in the nature of the current Arab boycott. I would argue that a firm stand by Canada against the boycott, a stand based on legislation of general application, is one way that Canada can contribute to the bringing of a peace, fair to all sides, to the Middle East.
To the extent that the rejectionist Arab states realize they cannot destroy Israel either through military or economic warfare, the more likely they are to agree to come to the bargaining table for face to face peace talks with the Israelis, talks of the kind that are presently going on between the Israelis and the Egyptians.
If the government wants to take a step, even though it might appear to be a small one, being that of only one country in the world community, that would help achieve peace in the Middle East, and if the government continues to be serious about what it said in the policy statement of October 21, 1976, then surely it must implement the two measures announced in it in the fullest possible way rather than in the most limited and narrow way. This, I regret to say, in my view is about all that it has done until now. But more important, it must act on recommendations like those of the Citizens' commission report issued early this year. This report demonstrated in particular the impact of the Arab boycott in Canada.

December 19, 1977
External Affairs
I would argue that the government must put into effect legislation against the boycott applying to all businesses, whether or not they need government support. If it does not do so, as I have pointed out, it is undermining its own policy on international boycotts. It is allowing foreign governments to extend their discriminatory law into Canada. This foreign law, after all, encourages one group of Canadians to discriminate for possible economic gain against another group of Canadians because of their origins and beliefs. This obviously clashes with Canadian standards of morality and human rights. Therefore, a Canadian federal law of general application is required so that no Canadian business would have to make its own decision as to the extent to which it should balance possible profit against ethics. Instead, all companies here would be on the same basis and none would have to fear losing business to a Canadian competitor if they follow the standards of conduct which the government, in its own policy statement, says are desirable and necessary.
Anyway, the evidence is clear that when a company does have the courage to refuse to comply with the boycott, either on its own or because of requirements of its own country's laws, generally the Arabs back down. If the goods or services are of a quality and price they are seeking, they will find a way of completing the transaction. Even if this were not the case and even if there were some marginal risk of economic loss, as I have said, I think most Canadians would want to see the government take a stand in a way that is in accord with the principles and ethics which provide the basis for our country's existence. The United States is finding it possible to do this in spite of much greater economic links with Arab countries than Canada.
General legislation for boycott compliance was adopted by the U.S. Congress earlier this year, and in spite of what those opposing it forecast, there has not been any breakdown as a result; there has not been any loss of U.S. trade with Arab countries as a result. Therefore, the question must be asked; how can Canada do any less if our government takes seriously the words of its own policy as announced last fall?
There are many similarities between the United States and Canada when it comes to social and economic systems. Canada and the United States are also major competitors in world markets. Surely the government can be asked: what is there about Canada that makes it less necessary and possible for it to have general anti-boycott legislation than it is for the United States? The United States already has trade and investment links with Arab countries far beyond anything we have now or contemplate for the future.
Like Canada, the United States is interested in expanding its trade with Arab countries. It is far more dependent on oil imported from them than Canada. As I have said, our two countries have similar systems of economic and social organization. The compulsory requirement in its law which the U.S. has had for some time, but which we do not have, which makes it necessary for firms there to report boycott requests and compliance with them showed a very high degree of such compliance. Therefore, when one bears in mind the high

degree of ownership of Canadian business by firms based in the United States, the conduct of Canadian companies, if not requiring government support for trade abroad, is not likely to be very much different.
Also, one can ask whether the standards and ethics of the United States, when it comes to affording its citizens the equal protection of the law against threats to their rights, like those created by the boycott, are higher in the United States than in Canada. I hope this cannot be shown to be the case.
The U.S. legislation is based squarely on the jurisdiction of the U.S. federal government under its constitution over international trade and trade between its constituent states. Our own constitution gives our federal government authority over international and interprovincial trade. There is, therefore, in my view, an equivalent basis under our own constitution for anti-boycott legislation along the same lines as that adopted by the U.S. Congress.
This new American law incorporates the concepts which President Carter said such legislation should have in order for him to give it his support as President of the U.S. In a statement before the law was passed he said that to have his support this law would have to contain, as it did:
Legislative language which would impose the following restrictions: Prohibit ail forms of religious or ethnic discrimination arising out of a foreign boycott- prohibit firms from refusing to do business with a country as a condition of doing business in another country-prohibit firms from acting as enforcers of a foreign boycott-prohibit firms from responding to requests for boycott-related information-prohibit the use of so-called negative certificates of origin within a year of enactment.
Such general legislation against the boycott was recently introduced, in fact just last week, by the Ontario government into the legislature of that province. This legislation indicates commendable intentions and it deserves wide community support. I am certainly not saying that about the government of Ontario in general. In other areas it certainly deserves to be replaced by the party led by Stuart Smith, but surely in this area it deserves wide community support.

The Ontario government, with its free enterprise, pro-business orientation, surely is as interested in encouraging Canadian trade abroad as is our federal government. Surely it would not be presenting legislation to the Ontario legislature that harms prospects of trade with Arab countries by residents of Ontario, whether companies or individuals.
To conclude, let me say that I think Canadians generally would join me in calling on the government for full and meaningful action to put its policy statement into effect in a way that fully protects Canadian civil rights and Canadian sovereignty. In order to maintain our national unity surely our national government must demonstrate that it can provide, and in fact is providing, security in economic and human terms to all its citizens, whether they are English-speaking or Frenchspeaking, and of every origin. Therefore, we and all Canadians as part of this effort must make sure the government takes meaningful action on issues such as the necessisty of preventing threats to that security like the Arab boycott. Such action
December 19, 1977

must be an important segment of a total priority effort by the federal government to preserve Canada as one, strong, united country serving the best interests of all its people, a country living in security, freedom, and prosperity in a peaceful world community in which Canada plays a full and useful part.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, reference has been made by previous speakers in this debate, notably by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), that this is the first time in 17 years that this House has had an opportunity to have a debate of this length on Canadian external relations. That is a surprising and disturbing fact. In fact I would categorize it as unbelievable, if it were not true, and certainly extraordinary and incredible.
In those 17 years how many matters have been stored up, seeking expression in this House? We have already had, aside from the tours d'horizon of the first two speakers, comments on nuclear proliferation, international aid, international research and development, and the Arab boycott. I myself have a great series of topics upon which I would like to comment, but I promise to be selective.
Seventeen years means that we go back to 1960, a significant date. It is also significant that it took pressure from this side of the House to get this debate going at all. I only hope that it will not take another 17 years before we have another debate on this subject. If I personally, or my party, have anything to do with it, we will not have to wait that long. In my view we should have debates of this length and breadth at least annually, and perhaps even more often.
In addition to the matter of the extended gaps between debates, but perhaps as a function of those gaps, I find it unfortunate that this government should decide to make surprise announcements in a debate of this kind, as it did this afternoon. I refer to the announcement on the subject of South Africa. While the government was at it, I wonder why it did not feel moved to make an announcement about the denial of human rights in Uganda, another part of Africa, where the tyrannical regime of Idi Amin surpasses by an immeasurable degree any goings-on in South Africa. At least profitable employment is being offered to Africans in South Africa, whereas in Uganda there is a tribal tyranny over all other tribes, buttressed by supporters, I am lead to believe, from outside the country. What is our aid package for Uganda? It is not easy to find out, but we should know what our aid package for Uganda is as a matter of course.
In any event, as to unilateral declarations of policy in the foreign field on whatever subject, surely these are matters about which inter-party consultations ought to take place. This is no matter for partisan politics, at least by my standards, but rather one to which a bipartisan or multipartisan approach ought to be adopted.
The government has learned nothing in the years in which it has been in office about the need to be more open in its handling of foreign affairs. I am confident that when the Conservatives are returned to power there will be a disposition
External Affairs
to take other parties into their confidence in the development of foreign policy measures. I do not say all matters, but at least in the matter of foreign policy, which is an area in which openness can and ought to be practiced.
We are asked to respond to the exhortations contained in the motion now before us, and I will read it now:
That this House takes note of the present state and future prospects of Canada's relationships with the other nations of the world.
How can we take note of the present state of our relations with the other nations of the world if we do not know what they are? In this general area of secretiveness I think one of the most outrageous examples of the way in which this parliament and the Canadian people have been treated can be found in the current negotiations with the United States on our maritime boundaries.
This country has no idea of what exactly is being negotiated, although we were assured as recently as this afternoon that, with an extension of another month the two, negotiators will come up with satisfactory results. What kinds of results covering what kinds of problems will they come up with? We should know. It has all been left to government appointees; competent ones, no doubt. One in particular I can speak very highly of; the other I do not know. However, some people have been denied an input, as my leader said earlier today, and those people are the most vitally interested parties, namely, the fishermen themselves.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext: They are involved.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext: Just about one year ago Canada took a momentous step by declaring Canadian jurisdiction for fisheries management out to 200 nautical miles. What has been accomplished in the intervening year?

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext: A lot.

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext:
We have adopted, for fisheries purposes, something more than one million extra square miles of sea, equal to about one third of our territorial surface area, yet we have done little to show that we are serious about taking care of our new acquisition or to provide in meaningful terms evidence of our assertion of this extended jurisdiction.
A great number of problem areas has been opened up. A few arrests have been made on both coasts. Negotiations have been going on with our neighbours, but no extra surface patrol craft have been ordered. We only recently concluded arrangements for air patrol craft. We do not really know how much further ahead we are today than we were this time last year or whether in fact we have derived any benefit from the action taken last January.
I would like to put forward this evening some ideas about what I think we should have been doing and what we should now be doing to ensure that we derive maximum benefit from the action taken January 1 of this year of extending out to 200 nautical miles Canada's jurisdiction over fisheries resources. Canada's action a year ago, possibly because it was taken

December 19, 1977
External Affairs
without too much forethought and planning, has had wide and profound international repercussions with which we have still to come to terms. I suggest that one of the most demanding tasks is working out satisfactory arrangements in a number of areas with our nearest neighbour, the United States, with which, incidentally, we have four complex boundary problems emanating directly from that 200-mile jurisdiction declaration.
I know discussions have been going on with Marcel Cadieux, our former ambassador to the United States, who is heading the Canadian team. We are assured that these discussions are going to lead to satisfactory results and that we will hear about them at the end of January. What are they intended to accomplish and how nearly are they accomplishing the ends? What goals are they setting out to accomplish? We have no knowledge of what matters are being considered in these negotiations, or how broad the discussions are. Do the discussions concern only boundary extensions? What effect are the proceedings going to have on other bilateral concerns?
Uncertainty and the muteness of the government on this matter prompt me to set forth a range of matters on which we should be negotiating, but about which we have learned nothing. The very fact that there is silence about the scope of negotiations, in itself, I suggest, is rather disquieting. On top of this uncertainty there is a positive certainty that oil shipments are coming down our west coast, and a search is being made for a port at which these shipments can be discharged. That is a certainty. In these circumstances it seems to me that a much more long-sighted approach ought to have been adopted and pressed with more energy.
For this purpose I should like to set out what I think ought to be included in any agreement with our United States neighbour, either as an umbrella agreement involving a great variety of matters connected with Alaska oil shipments and related issues, or a series of agreements each related to this wide spectrum of concern. I would suggest that at least the following matters deserve attention in any such agreement or agreements.
First of all, there is the fisheries jurisdiction; then compulsory traffic control including safeguards for fishermen and sportsmen; shipbuilding standards; crewing standards; cleanup facilities; clean-up cost settlement procedures, and finally, patrol. To be effective I suggest all of these should be included in any negotiations now taking place.
The main purpose underlying the extension of our jurisdiction to 200 miles was to gain management control over our fisheries. What we have established, in other words, is a fisheries management zone 200 nautical miles wide off our three coasts. If we had no neighbours nearer than 200 miles such an action would cause no great problem. But we do. Moreover, they have extended their jurisdiction, for fisheries purposes also, to the same width-although they waited two months after the Canadian action to take theirs. By March 1, 1977, however, the two zones were in place.

Where we first run into trouble in this double, unilateral action, is the interface between these two zones. Unfortunately there are four such interfaces, each with distinctive problems-one on the Pacific between British Columbia and the state of Washington, where the two extensions push out into the Pacific; the second, also on the Pacific, but this time between British Columbia and Alaska, again where the two extensions bulge out Pacificwards; the third in the Arctic, between Alaska and the Yukon; and the fourth on the Atlantic, between New Brunswick and the state of Maine.
As I have said, the problems posed by the extension of these four boundaries are separate and distinct. A single approach, in terms of agreement of a particular method of extending the boundary, does not seem to be possible-a median line approach may be feasible at one interface, a sectoral approach may be required on another, while an ocean-floor fault-or chasm-may be the best method of dealing with a third. On one, at least, there is already some uncertainty or difference of opinion, as to the meaning of the existing internationally agreed line established through arbitration. On one side it is viewed as a shore line and hence amenable to the creation of a band of a territorial sea; to the Canadian side that line is considered as an unmistakable boundary defining the limits beyond which the other's territory and territorial jurisdiction do not and cannot extend.
I wonder if, in the absence of agreements on these four important interface areas, there has been a chance to look at a bilateral agreement in which the sectoral approach might be applied, that is, applying the pie slice principle, carving out an area whose apex would begin at the internationally recognized seaward point with the two sides of the isosceles triangle or extending seaward for 200 miles, and that within that sector there be a joint jurisdiction exercised over fisheries, both management and take, as well as over pollution control measures.
As I see this approach, it could lead to an agreement under which each country would have an equal voice on the sectoral commissions that might have to be set up, and would give us four pie slices separating our respective 200-mile zones in those four areas where our zones would otherwise meet. In such circumstances the boundary, in its normal internationally accepted sense, between our two areas would subsequently have to be decided without regard to fish and pollution, but be concerned exclusively with other matters. For example, navigation, resource ownership, customs and immigration control, and military or naval matters might be amongst those things that would have to be separated by a single line. To do so, of course, would require explicit agreement spelled out in a bilateral convention-an umbrella agreement, in short, agreeing on the sectoral approach to deal with Fisheries and pollution plus accompanying agreements and subagreements defining the boundary for other purposes.
I have already suggested one reason for taking this sectoral approach to the resolution of our differences, namely, the difficulty we are probably having in deciding on a single boundary line to serve all purposes. Another is related to the
December 19, 1977

matters of common concern within that sectoral area-in particular because fish are no respecters of internationally accepted boundaries. Fishermen in pursuit of their livelihood follow fish migrations, or movements of schools. They might wish to do so across an international frontier and thereby risk getting into trouble with the neighbouring state. If, however, there were a common zone separating two distinctly national zones, and if, in that common zone, fishing practices-quotas, net sizes and so on-were agreed upon in advance, pursuit by the nationals of the two coastal countries into that common or shared zone would not render the fishermen concerned liable to prosecution, at least not until they passed out of it on the other side into the national jurisdiction of the neighbouring state.
That is one area of bilateral concern on which Canada and the United States should seek agreement, and possibly embed that agreement in a bilateral convention.
Since, however, the carriage of potential pollutants over these waters is of concern, because of the danger involved, to the fisheries involved, it is obviously desirable for the two neighbouring countries to reach some sort of agreement on how that commerce is to be carried out-in what kind of ships, with what kind of crews, and following what routes. Shipping standards, crewing standards and traffic control management must obviously be regulated along mutually agreeable lines. Double bottoms and twin screws for tankers might well be part of any such agreement, plus agreed seamanship qualifications for skippers and mates, not to mention mandatory traffic reporting procedures for all commercial vessels travelling into, out of, or through the area.
Another element in any such comprehensive agreement would be the storage of clean-up equipment and, quite as important, the establishment of procedures for dealing with the costs of clean-ups and claims arising from spills. This latter might have to envisage the creation of a fund into which vessel users would be required to pay and from which settlement of claims could be made. Whether a special court would have to be established for the settlement of claims is a matter that would obviously have to be examined most carefully. Whose law would prevail if the spill occurred in the "shared" zone? Would it necessarily be different from that prevailing in either of the national zones?
Finally, who would have responsibility for enforcement of the law set out in the bilateral agreement as it would apply to third nations? In this connection, it will be necessary to lay down specific principles governing patrol and surveillance responsibilities as well as authority to board, arrest, exclude or expel from the jointly administered area for infractions or suspected infractions. This is perhaps a new area of bilateral activity in the international arena but it is one into which we may well have to venture if we want to make the most of our 200-mile zone and at the same time achieve the elimination of a great number of friction points between our two countries. I believe we stand the best chance of maximizing the exploitation of our living respurces only if we proceed in such a
External Affairs
fashion, and I have gone to some lengths to set forth my reasoning for holding this belief.
I should like to deal with a number of other topics, but there are a number of other speakers who wish to take the floor. Before I sit down I do wish to underline the comment made just this evening about a drop in morale in the Department of External Affairs over the last several years, and more recently because of the split jurisdiction of the department. Now, there are four or five different ministers-the hon. gentleman over there may shake his head if he likes, but no one in the department knows who is responsible or who has the over-all responsibility-in other words, who is going to muck things up next. That is the problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. Norman A. Cafik (Minister of State (Multiculturalism)):
subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak here in the House of Commons on the question of human rights. I have in the last two and a half months addressed meetings from coast to coast, and on almost every one of those occasions I have spoken on the subject of human rights which so deeply affects Canadians, especially those of eastern European background.
It might come as somewhat of a surprise that a minister for multiculturalism should be dealing with a question of this kind in the House of Commons. However, as I view my portfolio it is not only vertical, in the sense that it deals with the legitimate aspirations and concerns of the ethno-cultural people of

December 19, 1977
External Affairs
Canada but it is also horizontal, in the sense that a great many of the things done by the federal government, provincial legislatures, and even municipal governments have an impact, positively or adversely on those concerns. The issue to which I intend to refer tonight affects literally millions of Canadians who come from eastern Europe or who are of Jewish origin, and who are particularly affected by what is happening in the Soviet orbit in terms of restrictions upon the exercise of human rights and the way human rights are abused and denied in that part of the world. I think it is important, too, to point out that Canadians of all backgrounds share this concern about encroachments on human rights because we in Canada, having taken our own human rights for granted for so long, do not look very kindly upon the violation of human rights in other parts of the world.
Not only have I spoken to groups across the country, I have listened to them as well and I have heard their cries of anguish and their expressions of frustration when they direct their attention to this subject. Some of them act on occasion as though the Government of Canada had complete control over what happens in foreign states. Obviously, they know this is not the case but in their concern for relatives and loved ones in their former home lands they grow impatient with their government and what is happening around the world. Their concern was very well illustrated the other night, on December 8, when I had the pleasure of speaking to the Canadian Ukrainian Professional and Businessmen's Association of Montreal.
A large number of Ukrainian people were present, but because I was in attendance they took the opportunity to invite some 40 representatives of 15 ethno-cultural groups in the city of Montreal. At the conclusion of that meeting, a large part of which was taken up by questions and answers related to human rights, they passed unanimously, or certainly with a great body of support, a resolution of which I received a copy in the form of a telegram. I should like to read that resolution in order to show the depth of feeling on the subject.
We the undersigned, being the representatives of various Canadian ethnic communities of Montreal, mindful of the difficult state of human rights in various countries of the world today and especially in Eastern Europe, hereby petition the Canadian federal Minister of Multiculturalism to state openly before the Canadian parliament the following resolution:
"Be it Resolved that the matter of human rights and the freedom of cultural expression shall be actively supported both within Canada and at all international conferences as a matter of Canadian government policy. More specifically and insofar as such rights and freedoms are consistent with our philosophy of the Canadian way of life and in accordance with the above, be it resolved that the Canadian government publicly denounce the official repressions of ethnic cultures and the intolerant treatment of dissidents in Soviet and eastern European countries today and that such a statement be forthwith publicly expressed by Canadian representatives at Belgrade to all nations presently there in international conference in review of the Helsinki Agreement.
Furthermore, be it resolved that consistent with the above the Canadian government take all necessary steps to successfully resolve all outstanding requests for family reunification and for immigration into Canada by persons desiring to make this country their new homeland."
Alexandre Biega, Q.C.,
Canadian Ukrainian Professional and Businessmen's Association.
(Mr. Cafik.J
That telegram, better perhaps than my own words, illustrates the great concern which Canadians from that part of the world feel about the way in which people are being treated in their former homelands. There are people who want to leave their homelands for family reunification purposes, and whose only crime is to stand up and act like free men in their own societies.
Literally thousands of dissidents in eastern Europe who have dared monitor the act which was signed in Helsinki are being persecuted in one way or another, and for a number of reasons, all of which boil down to a violation of their personal liberties and freedoms. These human rights violations, I suppose, exist in many countries of the world, but certainly they exist in overabundance in that part of the world. Now that the Final Act of Helsinki has been signed and we are presently in Belgrade reviewing the provisions of that Final Act, I think we have a new basis from which to speak out on this particular question.
Before making specific points with respect to what we ought to be doing, I should like to review briefly some of the provisions of the Final Act which was signed in Helsinki. It is important to go through some of the history, some of the hard, basic positions adopted in that Final Act, since I believe many Canadians were frustrated when Canada originally signed the Final Act. They were frustrated because they felt that this government and other western governments which signed the Final Act at Helsinki had solidified the existing boundaries of states within the Soviet orbit. That is not really the fact, Mr. Speaker.
The fact is that in that Agreement on Security and Co-operation in Europe there is provision to recognize existing boundaries in the sense that no one would use physical force to change the boundaries. That is quite different from giving some moral sanction to those particular boundaries which, in reading the accord, I do not find directly or even implicitly.
So far as the three Basket clauses of the Helsinki accord are concerned, let me deal first with Basket I. This section deals with ten fundamental principles. Nine of these deal with state to state relations. The seventh of the ten deals with a state's conduct toward its own citizens, namely, the question of human rights. The seventh principle states that participating states will respect human rights and fundamental freedoms: through conscience, religion or belief. It will encourage the exercise of political, social cultural and other rights; recognize the universal significance of human rights and fundamental freedoms as essential for peace and friendly relations among states. States will act in conformity with the United Nations Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and will also fulfil their obligations as nations to the International Covenants on Human Rights, dealing with economic, social and cultural rights, and civil and political rights.
Basket II deals with trade, industry, science and technology. It deals with the need to improve trade relations on the European continent. An important area deals with scientific
December 19, 1977

and technical exchanges involving the improvement of opportunities for the exchange and dissemination of information and international visits, including increased tourism on both and individual and group basis.
Basket III, which has more interest in relation to human rights for many in the west, is a provision which is the touchstone of the Final Act. The inclusion of humanitarian principles involving the freer movement of people, ideas, and information was a prerequisite of Canada and the western nations at the Helsinki talks. Basket III is essentially about international movement-the movement of individuals, information and ideas. Canada's main contribution in this particular area related to family reunification, which is a principle held so strongly by all Canadians.
Item one dealt with family reunification and emigration. Here states agreed to simplify the procedures and conditions for those requesting to leave in order to be reunified with families, and particularly with spouses, living in other states.
Item two dealt with regular family meetings. Here the agreement provides that states agree to attempt to ease the free movement among peoples, especially those who wish to meet with members of their families, and by promoting tourism and exchanges.
Item three was designed to increase circulation of printed, filmed and broadcast information and to improve the working conditions of journalists stationed abroad by freer travel and greater access to sources of information.
Item four dealt with cultural and educational exchanges in order to expand personal and institutional contacts by artists, scientists and scholars, and for access to information and materials.
I have run through those three Baskets in a very brief way in order to establish the background for the comments I will be making later on as to what in fact is happening in the Soviet Union and eastern European countries, so that we can relate those events to the sacred international agreement signed in Helsinki by those very countries. The major issues that I am concerned about are human rights, not only in eastern Europe but in all countries of the world.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) has in the past spoken in the House of Commons on the human rights climate in Uganda. There is no question that this is a serious concern and attracts a good deal of the attention not only of members of parliament but of all Canadians. The military coup against the democratically elected government of Chile and the subsequent arrest of individuals associated with, and sympathetic to, that government was another violation of human rights.
South Africa has been spoken of in this debate today. It is quite obvious that its official policy of apartheid is again a violation of basic fundamental human rights.
However, Mr. Speaker, these countries I have just named are not signatories to the Final Act signed in Helsinki. This does not make their violations of human rights any the less significant or any the less important, or indeed any the less
External Affairs
deserving of our attention as members of parliament or as Canadians. However, there is a distinction. The fact that they did not sign those accords, while the countries I am going to talk about in more specific terms did, makes a considerable difference. Therefore, monitoring all their abuses and publicly denouncing them, as a government, may constitute an interference with the internal operations of a foreign state.
However, in the case of the Soviet Union and other eastern European nations, they have agreed, by signing the Helsinki Accord, not only to monitor but to be monitored in regard to compliance within their own country of the Helsinki Final Act. Therein lies a very significant difference, because then for this country to speak out in relation to violations of human rights is not to interfere with the internal domestic affairs of a foreign state but, rather, to hold them accountable, as they would hold us accountable under this international agreement.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I think it is inappropriate for Canada or any other signatory to the Final Act, to be reluctant to speak out in Belgrade, here in parliament, or elsewhere in the world, in relation to perceived violations of that agreement. The Soviet Union's denial to its own citizens of the right to choose the country of their residence, is, if true, a violation of the Final Act, international agreements, and of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The Soviet Union's apparent lack of co-operation and its refusal to allow families to be reunited appears to be an abuse of basic human rights and of its commitment to the various accords and covenants which it signed, not only in Helsinki but in other parts of the world.
The Soviet Union continues to be restrictive concerning visits of relatives between our two countries. I am sure all members of parliament received communications about the difficulty of travelling back and forth between these countries, something which really is guaranteed under these agreements. The majority of those wishing to leave the U.S.S.R. on private visits to relatives in Canada do not appear to be getting out of that part of the world. Canadian tourists complain that travel within the Soviet Union is restrictive. They are not allowed to visit relatives in villages or the resting places of their forefathers at cemeteries.
Basic human rights and fundamental freedoms have been recognized as having universal significance and are the subject of international concern by the United Nations Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the Convention against Discrimination in Education, and The Final Act at Helsinki.
The Final Act recognizes the international significance of human rights and the responsibility which all signatories have toward defending these rights and freedoms. By signing the Final Act the Soviet Union recognized that compliance with the human rights obligations is fundamental to security and co-operation in Europe.

December 19, 1977
External Affairs
With regard to the Belgrade conference, Canada has taken a serious view of what is happening there and of our obligation to speak up in Belgrade in recognition of our obligations as signatories to the Helsinki agreement.
From the opening Canadian statement by Mr. Klaus Golds-chlag on October 6, 1977, I will take a few random quotations in order to illustrate the strong and positive position that the Government of Canada has taken in these meetings. I might point out that these are individual quotes and are not to be read in sequence. I quote:
We cannot proceed on the assumption that relations between states can remain unaffected where respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms is seen to be deficient... We cannot agree that such a discussion (on human rights) constitutes an intervention in the internal affairs of participating states. We are here to measure progress . .. The dispositions of the Final Act in the matter of human contacts are of special concern to Canadians. We are a country of settlement.. . (and) have continuing family links in Europe. The Canadian government has pursued a policy that attaches priorities to the reunification of families ... It is our hope that one of the results of our meetings will be a more generous and humane interpretation of the family reunification clauses of the Final Act, not as an exception but as a matter of general policy and practice . ..
If that were achievable here at Belgrade, it would help more than anything else to lend credibility to our efforts in the eyes of Canadians ...
Indeed the factor of credibility could be crucial to public support for detente in Canada-
It is quite clear that we have taken a strong position in relation to the Belgrade conference, and we shall continue to do that.
I want to move specifically to cases of problems that have been expressed by many Canadians of violations of human rights around the world. I would first like to talk about what is happening in the Soviet Union and in other parts of eastern Europe as a result of the Helsinki Accords. When the accords were originally signed, I understood the Soviet Union widely distributed copies of them. They felt it would substantiate and support their position at home. When it became widely distributed within the Soviet Union and in eastern Europe, groups of people sprang up to observe the implementation of these accords.
One, the Moscow group, was established on May 12, 1976. Its aim was to promote the observance of the humanitarian provisions of the Final Act by means of informing all heads of state which signed, and the public, about cases violating the articles in Baskets I and III. Prominent members of the Moscow group were arrested, including Yurii Orlov and Alexander Ginzburg. In fact on February 15, 1977, the House of Commons passed a unanimous resolution protesting those particular arrests. Later, Mr. Anatoly Shcharansky was arrested. I understand he was part of that monitoring group in Moscow. He has been held in prison without charge for nine months as of December 15, 1977. I understand the Soviet Union has acted to hold him a further six months without laying a charge.
The Shcharansky case is a very high profile one in which I became involved. On December 10, 1977, I had a meeting in Toronto with relatives of Anatoly Shcharansky who are citizens here in Canada. There are over 30 of them.
Following negotiations with the Department of External Affairs and others here in Ottawa, I went to Toronto to meet with them to see if they would support a proposition whereby we would allow immediate landed immigrant status to Anatoly Shcharansky in order to relieve the Soviet Union of the difficulty they had in this case. His relatives here in Canada supported that proposition so much so that they were willing to provide joint support for any application of landed immigrant status. No official response has yet been received from the Soviet Union. It is time that the government gave consideration to further action in this connection so that the Shcharansky family and all Canadians will know that we in Canada do not take violations of human rights lightly.
Anatoly Shcharansky is but one very important dissident. There was a group set up in Ukraine on November 9, 1976, to achieve the same objective, namely, monitoring the application of the Helsinki Agreement. Prominent members of the Ukrainian group who were arrested included Mykola Rudenko, Oleksii Tykhyi, Myroslav Marinovych and Mykola Matusevych.
A public group was formed in Lithuania on November 25, 1976. Groups have been established in Georgia, in Armenia and, I am sure, in other parts of eastern Europe to monitor the application of the Final Act. These people have been prepared to risk their lives, certainly their freedom, in order to defend the right of citizens in those countries to exercise their basic freedoms.
We have seen from the recounting of the Helsinki Accords that we not only have signed an agreement along with Soviet Union and other countries which allows us to be monitored for any violations of human rights in our homeland, but the right to monitor through the Belgrade conference and through other means the implementation of that agreement. If we have that right as a nation under this agreement, how can we do anything other than support those in countries who are doing that which we have the right to do under international agreements? It is only logical not to interfere in the domestic affairs of another state. In fact, however, we are fulfilling the obligations imposed upon us by being signators of that agreement, by speaking out and by drawing attention to these matters at Belgrade, in this parliament, in Canada, and throughout the world. We are drawing attention to violations that have occurred and that continue to occur within that part of the world.
We have a deep and solemn obligation to speak out on this matter. Canada should not interfere with the domestic affairs of another nation. Those domestic affairs should be respected, but our respect for the domestic integrity of a nation does not mean we have to violate our decent and basic respect for the human rights of citizens in any country of the world.
