speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CANADA'S RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, largely I want to direct my remarks to the coming United
[Mr. Cafik.)
December 19, 1977

Nations special session on disarmament. 1 hope the House appreciates this is one of the most important meetings that the United Nations has held since the Second World War.
Before doing so, I wanted to comment briefly on some of the remarks made in this debate today. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). I do not think many people in this Chamber could disagree with his very noble sentiments concerning how to move forward to a more peaceful world. I was surprised with one comment he made concerning Canadian-United States relations. He indicated that these relations had been handled adversely by the government and were at an abrasive state. When one looks at that question, one has to look at specific issues between Canada and the United States.
Is the hon. member suggesting that Canada's stance on the negotiation of boundaries should be more co-operative? Is he saying, for example, that on the Garrison diversion project we should have backed off in order to salvage Canadian-United States relations? Should we give up on the interception of salmon in the Fraser River by United States fishermen in order to maintain good relations? It takes two to maintain those relations. Canada has not been aggressive enough in dealing with the United States over cross-border issues, but we have not blown the question of Canada-United States relations.
We are two sovereign nations, and the evidence indicates that we must act in an independent manner. That is particularly the case with regard to the United States, because of the great unequal positions of power there are between the two countries.
I endorse what the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) said concerning the Arab boycott. He has expressed the views of the New Democratic Party on that particular subject. He should not get carried away with the question of refugees. There are three million Palestinian refugees in the world as well. I do not suppose he was suggesting that Canada should open its doors to them. Perhaps he was.
There is a real problem in the Middle East. Hopefully progress is being made in regard to that very abrasive conflict at this point in time.
We must stop being selective about human rights. My party supports the release of Anatoly Shcharansky. We would like to see more done in a public way for dissidents such as Daniel Schumacher in the Soviet Union. Also we would like to see an aggressive attitude on the part of this government in support of the victims of totalitarian regimes in Brazil, Chile, and the various other totalitarian states around the world. We cannot constantly deal with one question, the question of the victims of the Soviet Union. We have to look at oppression wherever it exists. Canada cannot be selective on the question of human rights. I am hopeful more and more names will come forward publicly from all over the world.

speechtext:
1 should like to refer to the United Nations special session on disarmament, particularly in regard to Canada's stance at that important conference. The United
Adjournment Debate
States has developed the capacity to destroy the Soviet Union some 36 times over with the amount of nuclear weaponry it now has in its hands. On the other side of that equation, the Soviet Union can destroy population centres in North America some 12 times over with the amount of nuclear capacity that country holds. That has contributed to peace in the world since the Second World War. Any objective observer will come to the conclusion that the absolute insanity and madness of a nuclear exchange has resulted in no nuclear exchange among the major powers. It is called "mutual assured destruction".
Canada should examine very carefully how it can go about not increasing the insanity of overkill and how something positive can be done to persuade other nations in the world, as well as ourselves, to move toward a position of reducing present massive expenditure on world armaments.
As a world power, Canada has a relatively modest defence budget. In fact not many people are concerned about this area of peace, the amount of our national budget which is directed toward matters of defence. My party does not object to reasonable expenditures for improving and upgrading some of the equipment, but we have serious objection to the kinds of equipment and the kinds of roles we are playing. We are concerned with the real question as to how much of our money is spent on surveillance aircraft for the 200-mile zone, and as to whether the F-16 is a useful expenditure for this country. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-ALLEGED ILLEGAL OPERATIONS OF BANK OF MONTREAL IN VANCOUVER- REQUEST FOR REPORT OF INVESTIGATION
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-ALLEGED ILLEGAL OPERATIONS OF BANK OF MONTREAL IN VANCOUVER- REQUEST FOR REPORT OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 5 I raised a question regarding a constituent of mine, Mr. Larry McHale, as I have done on several other occasions in this House. It is a case that I have followed with some interest and with some deepening concern to make certain that Mr. McHale receives justice.
Approximately two years ago Mr. McHale asked that an investigation be conducted into the activities of the Bank of Montreal and its handling of his account vis-a-vis an organization known as Argon Developments, together with a Mr. Percy. It strikes me that Mr. McHale is not the kind of person who is bent on any kind of wrongdoing.
I do not want to frustrate the normal course of justice in any way, but I want to help bring about justice as speedily as possible. In order to do that, I believe Mr. McHale deserves to be heard as quickly as possible.

December 19, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Obviously I do not know all the details of the McHale case and I do not even know whether in his dealing, corporate and otherwise, he has been guilty of any kind of civil crime, and I do not pretend to know. But I do know that on the evening of December 7 five members of the commercial crime section in Vancouver spent two hours in the McHale residence and buildings on his yard looking for evidence, apparently explosives, which would implicate him in a conspiracy to do criminal mischief against one of the corporations in Vancouver. They found nothing, but they arrested Mr. McHale. Two days later another officer came with a police dog and conducted a second search. Again they found nothing.
On December 10 I attended a bail hearing in Vancouver to see if bail could be established for Mr. McHale to allow him his freedom. I was struck by the incredibly sloppy work done by the Crown prosecutor at those hearings. His information was not accurate and he made allegations which were completely unsubstantiated and easily disproven. I was also struck by the prosecutor's attempt to link Mr. McHale in a tangential way to a Mr. Jim McCann who allegedly has been indiscreet in his talk and in his actions.
The prosecutor's actions and the arrest warrant based on the word of an informant lead me further to wonder about procedures against Mr. McHale. The informant who gave the information for the warrant is a man who has a criminal record as long as my arm. He has had several charges of breaking and entering and armed robbery, and now is charged in Burnaby with trafficking, and in Vancouver with possession of narcotics. Apparently on the basis of information from this kind of an informant, McHale is now being held without bail, almost totally incommunicado. His wife has not seen him since that day, except in the court room, and three days ago there was a third search of his property, and again nothing was found.
Over the past 15 months I have talked with Mr. McHale a number of times and have never found him to be oriented toward violence but always looking for a solution by means of the court. While he has mentioned some bizarre incidents of harassment in the past, he almost chuckled at them because he knew I would not believe them. Yet, just today I read again the Canadian Bill of Rights which includes:
The right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law.
Last night I received a phone call from Mr. McHale's wife, who was alone in the house with their three children. She told me that a brick had smashed through the window. I presume this is one of the bizarre incidents of the kind he had mentioned to me before.
I am coming to some very unwelcome conclusions regarding Mr. McHale's case. It seems to me that one of the unfortunate circumstances is that, while Mr. McHale is in prison without bail, he cannot even pursue the process of justice in his own case. It seems to me that justice is being frustrated there. Here is a man who feels he has been wronged by a major bank and
[Mr. Fricscn.J
be has been very vigorous in trying to have his grievance aired and judged. I am now beginning to wonder if he has been singled out for cruel and unusual punishment, both to discourage him and to make him an example to others. Therefore I urge that Larry McHale be given the speedy trial he has requested.
Canada has prided itself on being in the vanguard of civil rights, and I assume that this House and the judicial system in this country would want to see Larry McHale have a speedy trial and to see his case heard as quickly as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rod Blaker (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-ALLEGED ILLEGAL OPERATIONS OF BANK OF MONTREAL IN VANCOUVER- REQUEST FOR REPORT OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might first respond to the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) by explaining that the RCMP have indeed investigated the matter and that the resulting information has been relayed to the proper and appropriate authorities at the attorney general's office of British Columbia.
I also want to say that I very sincerely recognize the desire of the hon. member to pursue that principle of any open and free society that justice not only be done but that it be seen to be done. A more recent development of that adage might be that justice be done and seem to be done with reasonable speed.
I recognize the problem the hon. member raises, but I want to explain on behalf of the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) and his department that once a matter involving a criminal charge has come into contact with a provincial system of administration of justice it would be totally improper if any person on behalf of, or involved with, the Department of the Solicitor General were to intervene. In that connection I am pleased to say that I have had an opportunity to get some better understanding of the situation from the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock and that I appreciate all the more the concerns he has raised.
I am very strictly limited as to the type of involvement I might have, but within that stricture I am pleased to say to the hon. member that if there is any assistance I can give within the limitations I have just described in terms of the administration of justice, I will certainly be pleased to do so. In the meantime the proper answer has been given; that the matter is within the administration of justice, which is a provincial matter. I ask the hon. member's appreciation of the fact that administration of justice is not a federal matter but completely provincial.

subtopic: MANPOWER-BILINGUAL POSITIONS-REASON SOME EMPLOYEES DO NOT RECEIVE BONUS
MANPOWER-BILINGUAL POSITIONS-REASON SOME EMPLOYEES DO NOT RECEIVE BONUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 8 I addressed a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) asking about his awareness of a difficult situation which exists in the offices of his department in the Montreal region. I addressed my question to the minister based on a circular which was distributed in September by
December 19, 1977

the Treasury Board, and I would like to read a few sentences from it as follows:
The concept of units working primarily in French will be retained but the decision as to where such units will be organized will rest with individual departments ... The language requirements of positions will be based on the specific and actual work related need for one or both official languages.
Managers will determine the language proficiency required in bilingual positions for each skill (reading, writing, listening and speaking)...
At the same time the Public Service Commission issued a communique, and again I will read two sentences from it as follows:
Modifications to the official languages policies and programs of the federal public service will result in increased responsibilities for departments and agencies.
In the area of staffing, departments and agencies will now be responsible for determining the level of linguistic proficiency required of incumbents of bilingual positions within their jurisdiction.
In the constituency of Vaudreuil we are experiencing considerable difficulties in three departments. Under the Department of Veterans Affairs at the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital many of the patients are unilingual English and many of the patients are also unilingual French. It is, of course, necessary for the staff to speak both languages. We thus encounter considerable difficulty in that there are apparently certain percentages which are given for the various levels of persons who are to be designated as bilingual and therefore eligible to receive the bonus of $800. It is inevitable in such circumstances that there are people who must use both official languages but who will not receive the bonus paid to their fellow employees. This may create a difficult morale problem at this particular hospital.
Also in the constituency, which is about 50 per cent Frenchspeaking and 50 per cent English-speaking, we are obviously going to run into difficulties in the Post Office where once again service must be provided in both official languages. In the province of Quebec the language of work is French so once again, because of percentage restrictions not all the personnel that must service the public will be designated, and therefore not all the personnel will receive the bilingual bonus. Again, this causes discontent.
My question was addressed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration because of the situation peculiar to the west islands of Montreal where almost the entire population is English-speaking. Because the offices of this department are in part of the greater Montreal area, however, the language of work is French-and quite rightly so-but obviously necessarily the personnel dealing with the public must be able to speak the English language.
The case that I brought to the attention of the minister, asking whether he was aware of it, was typical of that obtaining in many of the offices. Six counsellors worked together, each counsellor being given responsibility for certain trades. The work of the counsellors does not overlap. Thus, depending on the trade of the person seeking employment, that person would be serviced by one of the six counsellors. Since 85 per
Adjournment Debate
cent or more of the clients in the office are English-speaking, it is therefore essential that all six counsellors speak the English language. Because of percentage restrictions, however, only five can be designated bilingual. The five receive the $800 bilingual bonus, and the sixth, who is extremely competent and fluently bilingual, does not receive the bonus. This obviously creates inequity and morale problems.
In the same office an individual has been transferred from Toronto. This individual works with English-language clients and is unilingual English. Although the individual is taking the French course and trying hard to speak the French language, certainly at the present time by any stretch of the imagination that individual could not be considered bilingual. Again, the language of work of this office is French so there is no possibility that this person can be designated unilingual, which would have to be unilingual French. This person must therefore fill a bilingual position and becomes eligible for the $800 bonus. Again, one can see the difficulty that has been created.
While understanding what the Treasury Board and its hardworking president has been trying to accomplish, it seems to me that he has effectively passed the administration of the program over to the departments and to the employees of those departments.
I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration about his knowledge of the situation. In his reply he tended to refer me back to the Treasury Board. I should like to hear tonight whether the document issued by Treasury Board in September which gives responsibility for administration to the departments, is actually in effect. I should like to know whether the employees are responsible and whether in these circumstances they are willing to investigate these particular examples of difficulty that are causing morale problems in my constituency.
Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the hon. member that the revised policy on official languages states that the bonus shall be payable to all eligible employees for whom the Treasury Board is the employer, as well as to governor in council appointees, when such employees occupy positions which have been identified as bilingual and the individual employee has been indentified by the Public Service Commission as meeting the established language proficiency requirements for the position.
The government is fully aware that there are cases in which public servants occupy bilingual positions but rarely use both official languages, as well as cases in which people occupying unilingual positions are using both official languages from time to time.
It would seem, notwithstanding the circumstances which the hon. member has described as being very strange, that if in fact there is an instance of one out of six persons in the area which he describes finding himself aggrieved by not having a bilingual position, upon the re-identification process taking place in the department in the hon. member's riding such an

December 19, 1977
Adjournment Debate
employee could then seek redesignation of his position as bilingual. This would be possible if he were able to show that the position required a bilingual person, and if he could also demonstrate that he was bilingual. Complaints of the same nature arising, say, in the Department of Veterans Affairs or in the Post Office could be handled in the same manner.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REASON PUBLICITY OF FEDERAL DEPARTMENT NOT BROADCAST
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REASON PUBLICITY OF FEDERAL DEPARTMENT NOT BROADCAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 29 last, I asked a question of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion about the advertising campaign made on private networks in Montreal but not on the CBC. The minister did confirm that such was the case despite the fact that he had asked the CBC to broadcast the paid advertising campaign. On December 16 last, I directed the same question to the Secretary of State responsible for the CBC (Mr. Roberts) asking him specific things: whether he was aware of the matter, if so whether he could advise the House about the result of his dealings with the CBC on advertising not broadcast on that network but on private networks. The Secretary of State answered as follows: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have raised the matter with the CBC and they are reconsidering the criteria involved.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, I took the liberty of doing some research, and I find that the CBC's drive to exclude paid advertisement from DREE was extended not only to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but also to the Post Office and the Department of Employment and Immigration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I went beyond those three departments and the one referred to in my two questions. I took the liberty of doing some further research, and I found two other departments where that unpaid advertisement had been broadcast by private networks, one case being an ad by the Department of Urban Affairs in Montreal concerning a project in our area that will certainly cost close to $1 billion.
The Department of Urban Affairs announced that another phase was being brought up to $63 million, to provide for water purification plants or network for greater Montreal. This was broadcast by private stations. Since then, Mr. Speaker, another minister, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport was in Montreal to attend an event that was non-political in my view, namely the Grey Cup Game. This got more than one hour's coverage time on private TV networks, but nothing on the government's network.
What concerns me deeply, Mr. Speaker, is that private networks are profit-making organizations. The Crown corporation is costing us over $500 million each year, and they are selective in their advertising. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary could be somewhat more precise than the minister, and answer those questions that are relevant in the current context. Canadians and certainly I myself would like to have
some explanation that would shed some light on the situation, because this goes much beyond the first question I put forward in the very specific case of one department. As I just suggested, this extends to six departments and, if I can follow up on my research, I am certain I will stumble on a good number of other cases.
Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, I take cognizance of the two questions put by the hon. member, and I would like to state that DREE's original message was rejected because the advertising copy went beyond the scope of straight information material and did more than present the department's expansion program for the Montreal area. However, Radio-Canada lately amended their policy concerning the acceptability of advertizing material and DREE's message was then considered as a simple documentary on the effects of the DREE expansion program in the province of Quebec.
All DREE texts have now been approved. The corporation has established standards for the programs stating views and the controversial texts which forbid it to sell broadcasting time for any advertising which professes opinions or leads to controversy. The only announcers which are acceptable are those who have definite goods or services to offer and the content of the advertising message must normally deal only with those goods and services offered. Any advertising originating from departments or federal organizations must present fact or information; it must not present questionable issues, nor engage in political proselytism, nor contain politically oriented comments or opinions.
Before this last revision of the commercial policy of the corporation, the clause which required that the message only contain facts or information was interpreted in the narrow sense as applying to the effective mechanisms of a particular program of action and not to the incidental benefits that might result from it.
The frame of this policy has now been enlarged to take into account the various types of government messages submitted to the CBC. There are for instance those messages broadcast to announce program or particular services, there are those texts containing persuasive material, there are reports showing attitudes and there are announcements of a more general character.
This broadening of the policy allows the presentation of programs, services and functions in a broader frame. However, the CBC notes that government advertising must still be free from any controversial opinions or any statement which would give support to a given economic, social or political view. Furthermore, messages originating from the government must not openly proclaim the achievements of the various departments of the government.
